newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China bank pullout to mar debt issues - analysts.
newsitem.headline: China bank pullout to mar debt issues - analysts.

text.p: Beijing's decision to force state banks out of the state debt markets operating under the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges will hurt the issue of government bonds, analysts said on Tuesday. The state banks have been told to transfer their debt trading to China's Shanghai-based local currency interbank market to stop bank funds leaking into the stock market.
Liquidity on the spot T-bill and repurchase (repos) markets in the two exchanges has dropped significantly as a result, analysts say.

"Turnover on the treasury debt markets fell by about one third last week due to the absence of the banks and it is very likely to continue to shrink," Liu Qinjian, a senior bond researcher at Shenzhen J&A Securities Co told the Hong Kong-based newsletter China Securities Bulletin.
"State debt offers are going to be a bit more difficult with the disappearance of the banks which are the biggest players," Liu said. "It could hit the enthusiasm of underwriters."

The central bank on Monday launched interbank state debt trading on the local currency interbank market, in which only banks that are members of the local currnncy interbank market, including 16 commercial banks and 11 urban cooperative banks, are allowed to conduct trading.

Non-banking institutions, including securities houses, trust firms and individual investors, will be restricted to trading on the markets on China's two bourses and smaller regional state debt trading centres around the country.
"The separation of banks from other investors means a split between the biggest sources of money supply and money demand, which creates an abnormal bond market," Liu said.
"Both the exchange-based and interbank market state debt trading will be stagnant as a result."

Chinese brokerages used to borrow funds from banks through repo markets on the two exchanges for speculative investment in domestic stock markets, which rose nearly 50 percent between January and May this year.
"The impact of the separation may not be too obvious over the short term but it is likely to become strong in the long run," another J&A Securities analyst said.
"Investors are becoming increasingly bearish about state debt contracts, with the banks leaving," an analyst at Shenzhen-based China Southern Securities Co said.
There is a contradiction between this move and China's intention to issue more government debt in the coming years, analysts said.
China is issuing about 250 billion yuan in state debt this year -- most of it domestic -- after issuing a record 195.2 billion yuan last year.
More than half of the 1997 debt has already been issued.

China needs to further increase T-bill offers to trim its budget deficit and to cope with a wave of government debt redemption and export tax rebates, the Shenzhen-based Securities Times said on Tuesday, quoting a report by the State Information Centre under the State Council, or cabinet.

China faces a 1997 budget deficit amounting to 50.08 billion yuan. It paid out 113.94 billion yuan in debt and interest in the first four months of this year, up 43.19 billion yuan or 61 percent from the same period in 1996, the report said.
"The size of state debt offers should be further expanded and we should prepare to reduce bond issue costs and boost liquidity on the secondary market," the report said.
"A depressed secondary market will have a direct negative effect on T-bill issues," it said.
